title: Molecular cobalt catalysts for electrocatalytic acetylene semi-hydrogenation

paper_content.abstract: Electrocatalytic acetylene semi-hydrogenation is an attractive route for ethylene production, but competing side reactions like hydrogen evolution, over-hydrogenation, and C–C coupling severely compromise its industrial viability. Here, we present a carbon-nanotube-supported metal phthalocyanine platform, MPc/XCNT (M = Cu, Co, Ni, Fe; X = O, N, S), to investigate the roles of metal centers and local coordination environments. Among these catalysts, CoPc-based structures exhibit markedly enhanced water dissociation kinetics and elevated C–C coupling energy barriers compared to conventional CuPc-based catalysts, thereby effectively suppressing undesired C by-products. Furthermore, molecular regulation of the Co center optimizes active hydrogen adsorption and utilization, mitigating both hydrogen evolution and over-hydrogenation. As a result, the optimized CoPc/NCNT catalyst delivers competitive performance under both high current densities and ethylene-rich conditions. At an industrially relevant −500 mA cm−2 under a pure ethylene feed, it achieves 86.7% Faradaic efficiency with a turnover frequency of 7019 min−1. Under simulated industrial crude conditions, it maintains 99.7% conversion and 99.5% selectivity during 110-hour continuous operation. This work provides a well-defined molecular strategy for advancing selective electrocatalytic transformations.
paper_content.introduction:
Ethylene (C2H4) is a vital feedstock in the chemical industry for synthesizing most commodity chemicals, including ethanol, glycols, and vinyl chloride1-3. Currently, most C2H4 is obtained by energy-intensive steam cracking of petroleum, and the C2H4 streams unavoidably contain trace acetylene (C2H2, 0.5−2 vol%) that poisons Ziegler−Natta catalysts in downstream polymerization and must be removed4-6. An alternative industrial route produces C2H4 by semihydrogenation of C2H2 derived from natural gas or coal7,8. In both cases, efficient and highly selective conversion of C2H2 to C2H4 is indispensable to meet the requirement of polymer-grade ethylene, where the residual C2H2 content must be below 10 ppm9-11. Nowadays, conventional thermocatalytic hydrogenation can reach over 99% C2H2 conversion and 90% C2H4 selectivity12-14. However, this process requires an excess of hydrogen (molar ratio of H2 to C2H2 >2), elevated temperatures (<100 °C), as well as high pressures (10-30 atm), which increases energy consumption and favours over-hydrogenation to ethane (C2H6)15,16. Electrocatalytic acetylene semi-hydrogenation (EASH) has recently emerged as a more sustainable alternative that uses water as hydrogen source and operates close to ambient conditions, and in principle can be coupled to renewable electricity and upstream ethylene production8,17-20. C2H4 yield and selectivity, however, remain limited by competing reaction pathways, including conventional over-hydrogenation to C2H6, carbon-carbon coupling to C4 olefins, and the emerging hydrogen evolution reaction (HER)21. Therefore, developing efficient catalysts that enhance selectivity, suppress side reactions, and operate at industrially relevant current densities is crucial for making this process viable.

As the EASH typically proceeds via the addition of adsorbed atomic hydrogen (*H, *corresponds to an adsorption site) generated from water dissociation, selective C2H4 production depends on both an appropriate hydrocarbon (i.e., C2H2, C2H4) adsorption affinity and efficient *H formation and storage22. Currently, Cu-based homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts have dominated the field23,24. To achieve an optimal hydrocarbon adsorption affinity that is sufficient to induce the reaction while still allowing easy desorption and avoiding overhydrogenation or C–C coupling, the local structure around homogeneous electrocatalysts has been modulated, such as surface orientation, cluster modification, heteroatom doping, et al., while for heterogeneous electrocatalysts, strain, alloy composition, coordination structure, and heteroatom functional groups have been engineered25-29. On the other hand, downsizing catalysts to the nanoscale to isolate active sites has emerged as an effective strategy to suppress competitive HER by limiting *H coupling. More recently, Zhang et al. demonstrated that nanosized Cu with rich unsaturated sites exhibits higher energy barriers for overhydrogenation, C-C coupling, as well as *H coupling compared to bulk Cu, enabling enhanced ethylene selectivity in EASH30. Yet even with these advances, complete suppression of C–C coupling at low overpotential remains difficult. A key limitation is that water dissociation on Cu surfaces is intrinsically sluggish and has recently been identified as the rate-determining step of EASH31. Thus, the rational design of catalysts that can balance selective hydrogenation and side reactions suppression remains an unmet challenge.

Metal phthalocyanines (MPcs), featuring a well-defined metal coordination environment, have been extensively studied for CO2 reduction, oxygen reduction, and HER32-34. However, their application in EASH remains underexplored. To date, only pioneering work by Zhang group35 firstly adopted bare CoPc and CuPc as electrocatalysts for EASH. Despite this initial progress, the influence of metal identity on EASH performance has been largely overlooked, leading most EASH systems to remain centered on Cu. Moreover, although the local coordination environment of MPcs is known to regulate their electronic structure, its role in governing EASH performance has yet to be systematically explored. To address these challenges, the MPcs supported on carbon materials provide a promising molecular platform, as their nearly square planar MN4 coordination unit offers a well-defined, tunable metal centre, and the macrocyclic ligand can be modified and immobilised on conductive supports while retaining a clear molecular structure.

In this work, we develop carbon nanotube-supported metal phthalocyanines, MPc/XCNT (M = Cu, Co, Ni, Fe; X = O, N, S), as a model platform to disentangle and exploit the function of the metal identity and local coordination environment in the EASH. Within the comparative MPc/OCNT series, CoPc/OCNT, NiPc/OCNT, and FePc/OCNT all exhibit significantly faster water-dissociation kinetics than the conventional CuPc/OCNT, thereby effectively suppressing undesired C–C coupling. This trend underscores the critical role of metal identity in facilitating water activation, which is essential for strongly suppressing C4 formation during acetylene semi-hydrogenation. Among these catalysts, Co-based catalysts exhibit the most effective suppression of C–C coupling but still suffer from severe HER at high current densities, which motivates further optimization of the Co sites. Guided by this insight, we then regulate the coordination environment of Co phthalocyanine through molecular interactions with nitrogen, oxygen, and sulfur functional groups on the CNT surface, where electron-withdrawing nitrogen functional group modulates the Co d-band center and generates optimized *H adsorption energy, elevating *H coupling barriers, and suppressing over-hydrogenation pathways, thereby mitigating HER and over-hydrogenation. The obtained CoPc/NCNT achieves >86.7% Faradaic efficiency (FE) for ethylene across a broad current density range (−50 to −500 mA cm−2), with ethane FE below 0.01% and no detectable 1,3-butadiene byproducts. Under simulated industrial conditions (5000 ppm C2H2 in crude ethylene), this catalyst maintains 99.7% acetylene conversion and 99.5% ethylene selectivity during 110-hour continuous operation, demonstrating good stability for scalable ethylene purification.
paper_content.results:
EASH performance comparison between metal phthalocyanines

The EASH performance of metal phthalocyanines was evaluated in a normal flow cell device with an electrode surface area of 1.0 cm2 under a 100% C2H2 feed, in which Hg/HgO and Pt foil served as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively, and an anion exchange membrane separated two chambers filled with 1.0 M KOH aqueous solution (Supplementary Fig. S1). The electrocatalytic acetylene hydrogenation performance of CoPc/OCNT and CuPc/OCNT was initially evaluated. Those two structurally defined catalyst models were rationally constructed following previously reported work (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. S2)36. Under an Ar atmosphere in 1.0 M KOH electrolyte, the LSV curves of the CoPc/OCNT catalyst exhibited an onset potential of −0.26 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE), approximately 30 mV more positive than the −0.29 V of CuPc/OCNT, and also delivered a higher current density across the HER polarization range (e.g., −87.5 mA cm−2 vs. −23.4 mA cm−2 at −0.6 VRHE), indicating its good water dissociation capability for generating reactive hydrogen species (Supplementary Fig. S2a); thus, under the C2H2 atmosphere, a more positive onset potential (approximately +100 mV) and higher current density of the EASH were observed on CoPc/OCNT as well (Supplementary Fig. S2b). The EASH process was then analyzed in the current density range from −50 to −500 mA cm−2 (Fig. 1b and c). For the CuPc/OCNT catalyst, the FE of C2H4 remained below ~50%, with C4 byproduct formation persisting at ~1.5%. In contrast, CoPc/OCNT achieved a significantly higher C2H4 FE of up to 90% with almost no detectable C4 byproducts, underscoring its superior ability to suppress C–C coupling (Fig. 1b).

To elucidate the reaction mechanisms, we performed online differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS). The C4H6 (m/z = 54) signal was absent on CoPc/OCNT, in sharp contrast to the prominent C4H6 signal observed on CuPc/OCNT, directly corroborating the C–C coupling effective inhibition of Co active sites (Fig. 1d and e). The H2 (m/z = 2) was detected at –0.28 V RHE on CoPc/OCNT, appearing 40 mV earlier than on CuPc/OCNT, while the C2H4 (m/z=28) signal for CoPc/OCNT emerged at –0.2 V RHE, 120 mV more positive than that of CuPc/OCNT. This trend is consistent with the ~30 and ~100 mV positive shifts in the HER and EASH onset potentials, respectively, from CoPc/OCNT to CuPc/OCNT observed in the LSV measurements. (Supplementary Fig. S2a). Moreover, one can see for CoPc/OCNT that the C2H4 signal emerged 80 mV earlier than the H2 signal, whereas for CuPc/OCNT, both signals appeared simultaneously, demonstrating the competitive advantage of CoPc/OCNT for EASH over HER. Kinetic isotope effect (KIE) studies (H2O/D2O) further validated accelerated water dissociation on CoPc/OCNT (kH/kD =1.48 vs. 1.62 for CuPc/OCNT), promoting more *H transfer to adsorbed *C2H3 intermediates rather than H2 formation (Fig. 1f)37. According to the following theoretical calculations, the d-band center of Co in CoPc/OCNT was calculated to shift closer to the Fermi level compared with that of CuPc/OCNT, likely strengthening the adsorption of critical intermediates (i.e., *H and *C2H3) and potentially facilitating rapid EASH (Fig. 1g). Subsequent analysis of water dissociation barriers suggests that CoPc/OCNT exhibited a theoretically lower barrier for H2O dissociation than CuPc/OCNT (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. S3). Therefore, the calculated facilitation of H2O dissociation not only could lead to higher HER activity under Ar, as the H2O dissociation-associated Volmer step is generally considered rate-determining, consistent with earlier LSV and DEMS results, but also, under C2H2, the theoretically rapidly generated *H is proposed to be preferentially consumed by hydrogenation of adsorbed C2H2, which, together with the elevated C–C coupling barrier and *H–*H coupling barrier (Fig. 1i, Supplementary Fig. S3 and S4), may explain the high C2H4 selectivity and the absence of detectable C4 products experimentally observed on CoPc/OCNT.

Accordingly, CuPc/OCNT and CoPc/OCNT follow distinct catalytic behaviors during the EASH process. For CuPc/OCNT, the rate-determining step is water dissociation, resulting in insufficiently active *H species, and its high susceptibility to HER further exacerbates this limitation. Therefore, both HER and *C2H3 coupling into C4 products inevitably occur, and HER becomes the dominant pathway even from relatively low current densities (> 50 mA cm−2, Fig. 1c). In contrast, CoPc/OCNT enhances *H availability through efficient water dissociation, and prioritizes EASH over HER, thus fully suppressing C4H6 formation. To assess the generality of this water-dissociation-governed suppression of C–C coupling, we also synthesised NiPc/OCNT and FePc/OCNT and evaluated them under identical conditions. LSV curves and Tafel slopes under Ar indicate that both NiPc/OCNT and FePc/OCNT promote water dissociation more efficiently than CuPc/OCNT (Supplementary Fig. S6). Quantitative product analysis at −100 mA cm⁻2 shows that the Faradaic efficiencies of C4H6 on FePc/OCNT and NiPc/OCNT are both below 0.15%, much lower than that of CuPc/OCNT (1.40%), which is consistent with the view that accelerated water dissociation helps to alleviate C–C coupling and C4 formation (Supplementary Fig. S7). Therefore, within this MPc/OCNT series, CoPc/OCNT exhibited the most effective suppression of C4 formation while maintaining high C2H4 selectivity. However, despite its high selectivity, CoPc/OCNT still suffered from significant HER side reactions at high current densities (> 300 mA cm-2), which limit its industrial applicability (Fig. 1b).

Tunable molecular catalyst design and characterization

To address the limitations imposed by competing HER, we introduce a tunable molecular strategy that electronically modulates the Co center to optimize its catalytic performance. Specifically, silane coupling agents bearing diverse functional groups, i.e., -NH2 and -SH, were grafted onto hydroxyl-rich oxidized carbon nanotubes through reactions with surface hydroxyls38. These agents follow the general formula X-R-Si-Y3, where Y represents hydrolyzable groups forming silanol, X denotes metal-coordinating functional groups, and R is the carbon chain linking X and Si. Thanks to these grafted agents, functionalized CNTs (XCNT, X=O, N, and S) could coordinate with metal atoms through strong electronic interactions mediated by the incorporated heteroatoms (Fig. 2a). Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy confirmed the presence of abundant hydroxyl groups on OCNT and characteristic -NH2 and -SH on NCNT and SCNT, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S8). Additionally, energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping demonstrated the uniform distribution of these functional groups across the XCNT surface (Supplementary Figs. S9–S11). These heteroatom functional groups, serving as axial ligands, could electronically regulate the Co center in CoPc through strong d–p orbital hybridization, leading to a uniform distribution of CoPc. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of CoPc/XCNT exhibited characteristic peaks of amorphous graphite, with no diffraction peaks corresponding to crystalline species of CoPc, indicating that there is no agglomeration of CoPc on the nanotube walls (Supplementary Fig. S12). Similarly, the Raman spectra of CoPc/XCNT showed the absence of CoPc vibrational bands in the 600–700 cm⁻1 range, further confirming the high dispersion of CoPc molecules (Supplementary Fig. S13)39. According to high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) characterization, the nanotube structure of XCNT was retained after CoPc loading, with no significant aggregation observed as well (Fig. 2b). The spherical aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscope (AC-STEM) image displayed the isolated bright spots on the walls of XCNT, confirming the successful loading of CoPc (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. S14). The elemental mapping via scanning transmission electron microscopy energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM-EDS) further demonstrated the uniform distribution of all elements in CoPc/XCNT (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Figs. S15 and S16). The inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) revealed comparable Co loadings on CoPc/OCNT, CoPc/NCNT, and CoPc/SCNT, measuring 0.55 wt%, 0.47 wt%, and 0.57 wt%, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S17 and Table S1).

The electronic regulation of the Co center in CoPc achieved through this molecular strategy was investigated using X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) characterizations. The O K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectrum of CoPc/OCNT demonstrated a cobalt-oxygen bond feature at 532.8 eV40,41, which was absent in bare OCNT (Supplementary Fig. S18a). In CoPc/NCNT and CoPc/SCNT spectra, the cobalt-nitrogen and cobalt-sulfur bonds were observed at 399.7 eV and 168-185 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S18b and S18c)42,43. The presence of these bonds clearly indicates that Co atoms in CoPc coordinate with X heteroatoms in XCNT through strong d-p orbital interactions. Furthermore, the high-resolution Co 2p XPS spectra exhibited slight shifts in both Co 2p3/2 and Co 2p1/2 peaks compared to the bare CoPc (Fig. 2e). In particular, the Co 2p3/2 binding energies followed the order CoPc/SCNT (779.1 eV) < CoPc (779.8 eV) < CoPc/NCNT (780.8 eV) < CoPc/OCNT (780.9 eV), indicating a gradual increase in Co valence from S- to N- to O-coordinated CoPc. This trend was consistent with the increasing electronegativity and decreasing electron-donating ability of the axial ligands from S to N to O, confirming that the Co electronic structure can be precisely tuned by the heteroatom-doped CNT support. To further elucidate the local coordination environment of Co in CoPc/XCNT, Co K-edge XANES and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analyses were performed. As shown in Fig. 2f, the near-edge absorption intensity of the Co K-edge for CoPc-XCNT was between those of Co foil and Co3O4, confirming that Co was in a positively charged state. All CoPc/XCNT catalysts exhibited a distinct pre-edge feature at ~7715 eV, which was characteristic of the 1s→3d transition of the square-planar Co–N4 center, demonstrating that the in-plane Co–N4 configuration of CoPc was retained on the CNT supports. Notably, the Co K-edge and pre-edge features exhibit a systematic energy shift that correlates with the specific heteroatom in the CNT support. Relative to pristine CoPc (7750.5 eV), the absorption edge of CoPc/OCNT shifts toward higher energy (7751.4 eV), whereas a significant shift toward lower energies is observed for CoPc/NCNT (7745.7 eV) and CoPc/SCNT (7744.0 eV). This energy hierarchy (CoPc/OCNT > CoPc > CoPc/NCNT > CoPc/SCNT) underscores the potent electron-withdrawing nature of axial O relative to N and S, which induces a higher Co oxidation state in CoPc/OCNT and a progressively more reduced state in the N- and S-coordinated analogues. These observations are in agreement with the XPS results. The Fourier-transformed EXAFS (FT-EXAFS) spectra of CoPc/XCNT revealed the absence of the Co–Co scattering path (2.2 Å) observed in Co foil, signifying that the Co species existed as isolated single-atom sites (Fig. 2g)44. For CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/NCNT, broad peaks were observed at 1.5 Å, attributed to the Co-N or Co-O bonds, whereas CoPc/SCNT exhibited two distinct peaks at 1.5 Å and 1.9 Å, corresponding to Co-N and Co-S bonds, respectively, revealing the dual-coordination structure. Additionally, wavelet-transform (WT) contour plot analysis corroborated the absence of the Co–Co coordination in CoPc/XCNT (Fig. 2i and Supplementary Fig. S19). Quantitative EXAFS curve fitting results for CoPc/NCNT showed two paths at 1.92 and 2.18 Å, attributed to the Co–N and Co–N scattering paths, respectively (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. S21 and Table S2). Moreover, the Co–N4O1 and Co–N4S1 configurations were confirmed for CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/SCNT, respectively. Overall, the above characterizations reveal the CoPc-like Co-(pyrrolic N)4 structure with X-atom modification in CoPc/XCNT, which significantly regulates the electronic distribution at the Co center.

EASH performance of molecular catalysts

The EASH performance of CoPc/XCNT was evaluated in a normal flow cell device with an electrode surface area of 1.0 cm2 under a 100% C2H2 feed. Initial performance evaluations in acidic, neutral, and basic electrolytes indicated that the alkaline environment is preferable (Supplementary Fig. S22), and thus, a 1.0 M KOH aqueous solution was chosen as the electrolyte for further studies unless otherwise stated. Compared with the CoPc supported on bare commercial carbon nanotubes (CoPc/CNT), most CoPc/XCNT catalysts significantly suppress side reactions and enhance selectivity, indicating the effectiveness of molecular regulation in enhancing EASH performance (Supplementary Fig. S23). The CoPc/NCNT showed a higher current density over the potential range from 0 V to −0.6 VRHE, as well as notably lower Tafel slope compared with CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/SCNT, indicating enhanced EASH kinetics over the molecular regulation (Fig. 3a and 3b). The product distribution of acetylene selective hydrogenation on CoPc/NCNT and CoPc/SCNT was also given across a current density range of −50 to −500 mA cm−2 (Fig. 3c-d and Supplementary Fig. S24). Note that the selectivity of C2H4 exceeded 99% on all CoPc/XCNT in the investigated current density range, verifying again that the isolated Co atomic site effectively suppressed C-C coupling processes. On CoPc/NCNT, the FE for C2H4 remained ~90%, reaching a maximum of 96.6% at a current density of −100 mA cm−2, while the byproduct C2H6, the product of the overhydrogenation reaction, had FE below 0.2%, and no C4H6 was detected. Impressively, at an industrial-level current density of −500 mA cm−2, the FE for C2H4 remained above 85%, continuing to fall within the profitable region and indicating the good economic potential of the CoPc/NCNT catalyst towards EASH19; in contrast, the FE for C2H4 on CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/SCNT dropped significantly to 17.5% and 4.7%, respectively. The variations in polarization curves and selectivity clearly indicated that the EASH kinetics and reaction pathway on CoPc/XCNT could be effectively tuned by regulating the electronic distribution at the Co center through X-atom modification. As a result, the CoPc/NCNT exhibited a high overall turnover frequency (TOF) value of 7019 min−1 at −500 mA cm−2 under pure C2H2 flow (Supplementary Note 1), which was increased by more than one order of magnitude in comparison with those of previously reported electrocatalysts (Supplementary Table S3). In addition, the CoPc/NCNT showed good catalytic stability. As shown in Fig. 3e, within 60 h of continuous operation at −100 mA cm−2, both the potential and the corresponding FE for C2H4 remained stable. Under a more demanding current density of −500 mA cm−2 in 1 M KOH, CoPc/NCNT still sustains an FE(C2H4) above 80% over 10 h of continuous operation (Supplementary Fig. S25). Post-electrolysis XPS and AC-STEM characterisation (Supplementary Fig. S26) showed nearly unchanged Co 2p features and only isolated Co sites without detectable nanoparticles or clusters, indicating that the CoPc-like single-atom configuration was preserved under EASH operating conditions. To rule out its potential contribution, the so-called electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) of CoPc/NCNT was evaluated. The calculated electrochemical double layer capacitance (Cdl) value of CoPc/NCNT was 19.3 mF cm−2, slightly higher than 16.6 mF cm−2 of CoPc/OCNT and 11.5 mF cm−2 of CoPc/SCNT, indicating its greater number of active sites. However, after normalizing by the obtained ECSA values, the EASH kinetic activity still followed the order of CoPc/NCNT > CoPc/OCNT > CoPc/SCNT, demonstrating that the performance enhancement primarily originated from the intrinsic activity of the active sites (Supplementary Fig. S27). In addition, the influence of CoPc loading was also examined (Supplementary Figs. S28 and S29). Notably, CoPc/NCNT with 5 wt% CoPc exhibited the highest EASH activity across various current densities. However, further increasing the loading to 10 wt% led to a decline in catalytic activity, likely due to CoPc aggregation. For flow cells, optimizing catalyst loading on the gas diffusion electrode (GDE) is essential to ensure sufficient acetylene reactants and active site availability. After adjusting the CoPc/NCNT loading on electrodes, the optimal EASH performance was achieved at a catalyst loading of 0.4 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Fig. S30). Therefore, unless otherwise stated, CoPc/XCNT with 5 wt% CoPc and a loading of 0.4 mg cm−2 was used in subsequent studies.

To validate the intrinsic catalytic sites, bare CoPc as well as CoPc-free OCNT, NCNT, and SCNT were employed for comparative analysis. The corresponding Faraday efficiency demonstrated much faster reaction kinetics for bare CoPc than OCNT, NCNT, and SCNT. The FE for C2H4 on bare CoPc was about 41.6% at −100 mA cm−2, much higher than 34.1% on OCNT, 6.2% on NCNT, and 12.3% on SCNT, respectively (Supplementary Figs. S31 and S32). Compared with bare CoPc, the XCNT substrates exhibited negligible acetylene semi-hydrogenation activity in both kinetics and selectivity, underscoring the pivotal role of molecularly dispersed CoPc sites in driving catalytic efficiency for EASH. This key role of CoPc was further supported by the LSV curves of NCNT and CoPc/NCNT under pure C2H2 flow, in which the markedly reduced performance in the absence of CoPc gave direct evidence of its catalytic contribution (Supplementary Fig. S33). When comparing the performance of bare CoPc with CoPc/XCNT catalysts, CoPc and CoPc/SCNT exhibited comparable reaction kinetics, both much lower than those of CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/NCCNT; the FE for C2H4 obtained at −100 mA cm‒2 followed the order: CoPc/SCNT (26.1%) < CoPc (41.6%) < CoPc/OCNT (91.2%) < CoPc/NCNT (96.6%). This performance trend is consistent with the regulation degree determined by the X heteroatom electronegativity (Fig. 2e and 2f). This consistency not only suggests that CoPc serves as the main active site while XCNT acts as its electronic modulator, but also highlights that the EASH performance is governed by the electronic structure of CoPc, which can be finely tuned through molecular regulation.

Mechanism of the high selectivity for ethylene

Before discussing the mechanistic role of molecular regulation, we first examined whether the enhanced activity of CoPc/NCNT could simply originate from changes in the physical properties of the carbon support. Four-probe tests show that the resistance increases from 0.018 Ω∙cm for CoPc/OCNT to 0.029 Ω∙cm for CoPc/NCNT and 0.086 Ω∙cm for CoPc/SCNT (Supplementary Table S4), indicating a slight increase in overall resistance. Contact angle measurements reveal that the surface becomes more hydrophobic, with the contact angle increasing from 65.5° (CoPc/OCNT) to 92.1° (CoPc/NCNT) and 96.4° (CoPc/SCNT) (Supplementary Fig. S34). C2H2-temperature programmed desorption results further show a gradual increase in C2H2 adsorption capacity (Supplementary Fig. S35). However, the EASH activity of the bare OCNT, NCNT, and SCNT supports remains low and in some cases even decreases after functionalisation (Supplementary Fig. S32). These results indicate that the high performance of CoPc/NCNT cannot be rationalised solely by favourable conductivity, hydrophilicity, or adsorption of the support, and instead mainly arises from the modified coordination environment and electronic structure of the Co centres induced by heteroatom doping.

To further elucidate the impact of molecular regulation on the reaction process, the EASH mechanisms of CoPc/XCNT catalysts were explored through a series of operando experiments. Operando Co K-edge XANES was used to probe the possible dynamic evolution of Co sites in CoPc/NCNT under working conditions (Supplementary Fig. S36). The spectrum at open-circuit potential resembles that of molecular CoPc and lies between Co foil and CoO, indicating a Coδ⁺ state between metallic Co and Co(II). As the applied potential becomes more negative, the absorption edge shifts progressively to lower energy and the white-line intensity decreases (Fig. 4a), showing that the Co centres become partially reduced during operation. Together with the negligible EASH activity of bare NCNT and the pronounced activity enhancement after introducing CoPc, it is safe to conclude that CoPc-derived Co centres serve as the primary active sites in CoPc/NCNT8. Subsequently, the EASH pathway on CoPc/NCNT and the associated interfacial water structure were investigated using potential-dependent in situ attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy. In the O–H stretching region, the broad band between 2900 and 3700 cm−1 can be deconvoluted into contributions from 4-coordinated hydrogen-bonded water (4-HB·H2O), 2-coordinated hydrogen-bonded water (2-HB·H2O), and K+-hydrated water (K·H2O). With increasingly negative potentials, the intensity of the 4-HB·H2O component decreases, while that of 2-HB·H2O increases, suggesting that the interfacial hydrogen-bond network becomes more weakly bound and that water dissociation is facilitated45, thereby increasing the availability of *H for the semi-hydrogenation of acetylene. In the lower-wavenumber region, positive bands at 1650 and 1559 cm−1 can be assigned to adsorbed *C2H2 and the generated *C2H3 intermediate on CoPc/NCNT, respectively. The intensity of the band corresponding to *C2H4 grows continuously with potential, consistent with the high ethylene selectivity observed on CoPc/NCNT (Fig. 4b). To determine the hydrogenation pathway in the EASH process, we systematically evaluated the origin and transfer of hydrogen through electrolyte-dependent experiments, including pH variation, scavenger tests, and cation effects. If the rate-determining step followed a proton-coupled electron transfer pathway of the form *C2HxHy + H2O + e- → *C2HxHy+1 + OH−, the EASH activity would display a pronounced sensitivity to pH or OH− concentration. The polarization curves and the C2H4 FE of CoPc/NCNT were then recorded in KOH solutions ranging from 0.5 to 5.0 M (pH≈13.7 to 14.7). With increasing pH, the polarization current density increases gradually, which can be mainly attributed to improved electrolyte conductivity and mass transport (Supplementary Fig. S37)8. In contrast, the onset potentials and the FE for C2H4 show no significant changes across this one-order-of-magnitude variation in OH− concentration (Supplementary Fig. S38). Such behaviour is not typical of a step controlled by proton-coupled electron transfer, and suggests that the key hydrogenation step does not directly depend on the bulk proton or hydroxide activity under the present conditions. The role of *H intermediates was further probed by adding tert-butanol (t-BuOH), a radical scavenger that deactivates *H via 2-methyl-2-propanol formation. Upon addition of t-BuOH, the polarization current density and C2H2 conversion decrease markedly (Supplementary Fig. S39). The combination of a weak pH dependence and a strong sensitivity to *H scavenging indicates that surface-bound *H, rather than a direct proton-coupled electron-transfer step, serves as the key reactive intermediate in the electrocatalytic hydrogenation of C2H2 on CoPc/NCNT46. Quasi-in situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy further reveals the formation of carbon- and hydrogen-centred radicals on CoPc/NCNT under EASH-relevant potentials, whereas no radical signal is detected at open-circuit potential (Fig. 4c). In strongly alkaline media, the proton concentration is negligible, which disfavors a proton-coupled electron transfer pathway. Taken together with the pH variation and radical scavenger experiments, these results are consistent with a hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) mechanism. Specifically, water-derived *H intermediates are preferentially consumed via sequential hydrogen transfer to adsorbed C2H2, which mitigates competitive HER pathways (in particular the Heyrovsky-type route) and enables selective semi-hydrogenation in the low-to-intermediate current-density regime. To further probe this water dissociation–hydrogen transfer pathway, we tuned the hydrated cations M+(H2O)n by introducing different cations. Large hydration numbers and effective ionic radii are expected to weaken specific interactions between cations and Co active sites. This effect was examined by substituting compact K+(H2O)7 (n=7, r=3.3 Å) and Na+(H2O)13 (n=13, r=3.6 Å) with more strongly hydrated Li+(H2O)n (larger hydration shell, r=3.8 Å) and bulky TMA+ (n=18, r=4.5 Å) in 1.0 M KOH electrolytes (Supplementary Fig. S40). Under these conditions, the EASH kinetics follow the sequence K+ > Na+ > Li+ > TMA+, with C2H2 conversion decreasing from 30.3% (K+) to 10.4% (TMA+)47. This trend can be attributed to the ability of the cations to perturb and disrupt the interfacial hydration shell. Namely, the relatively compact K⁺(H2O)7 cluster likely polarises interfacial H2O networks more effectively than more strongly hydrated or bulkier cations, thereby facilitating water dissociation and the formation of reactive *H species on CoPc/NCNT.

Accordingly, a reaction mechanism is proposed (Supplementary Fig. S41) that involves coupled H2O dissociation and C2H2 hydrogenation. First, C2H2 adsorbs on the CoPc/NCNT surface in a flat configuration. In parallel, K⁺(H2O)7 promotes rapid water dissociation at the CoPc/NCNT interface to generate active hydrogen species. The adsorbed *C2H2 then couples with *H to form the partially hydrogenated intermediate *C2H3. A second hydrogenation step converts *C2H3 into *C2H4, which subsequently desorbs from the CoPc/NCNT surface, regenerating the catalytic sites for the next reaction cycle.

The rate-determining step in the EASH process was further analysed by combining kinetic isotope effect measurements with HER kinetics under Ar. The H/D KIE, defined as the ratio of C2H4 formation rates in H2O and D2O (Fig. 4d), is 1.48 for CoPc/OCNT and 1.73 for CoPc/SCNT, indicating that water dissociation remains strongly involved in the overall rate on these two catalysts. In contrast, CoPc/NCNT exhibits a smaller KIE of 1.15, which implies a reduced sensitivity to H/D substitution and that water dissociation is no longer the dominant kinetic limitation48. LSV and Tafel analysis in Ar saturated electrolyte (Fig. 4e) yields a Tafel slope of 94 mV dec⁻1 for CoPc/NCNT, lower than those of CoPc/OCNT (127 mV dec⁻1) and CoPc/SCNT (158 mV dec⁻1), a trend typically associated with more facile water activation in alkaline media (Supplementary Fig. S42). Together, these results show that CoPc/NCNT possesses the fastest water dissociation kinetics among the three CoPc/XCNT catalysts and shifts the kinetic bottleneck away from the initial water splitting step. The following isotopic labeling experiments detected deuterium in both C2H4 and H2 when using D2O, further verifying water as the exclusive hydrogen source (Fig. 4f). To monitor hydrogen species utilization during the EASH process, online DEMS was then performed under LSV mode (Fig. 4e, g, and h). Under C2H2 feed, CoPc/NCNT exhibited a more negative onset potential for H2 evolution than CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/SCNT, which, in combination with the KIE results, suggested that CoPc/NCNT enabled faster *H generation and more efficient transfer to C2H2, resulting in the exceptional HER suppression and improved hydrogenation kinetics.

According to the above experimental observations, targeted DFT calculations were also conducted to provide insights into the possible molecular regulation of CoPc in facilitating the EASH process. Models of CoPc/XCNT were constructed based on the EXAFS fitting results. Stabilization of CoPc on functionalized graphene surfaces was suggested by negative adsorption energies, with axial X heteroatom (O, N, S) spontaneously coordinating Co via strong d-p orbital hybridization (Supplementary Fig. S43). Charge density difference analysis indicated that the modeled CoPc/NCNT exhibited moderate charge depletion at the Co center compared to CoPc/OCNT and CoPc/SCNT (Fig. 4i). Due to its varied electronegativity, i.e., O > N > S, axial X heteroatoms modulated d-orbital occupancy through electron withdrawal/donation, redistributing electron density, and spin polarization. PDOS calculations suggested a volcano-shaped relationship between Co d-band center positions and ligand electron-withdrawing capability, which likely influences reaction intermediate adsorption strength (Fig. 4i)49. Given the predominant competition from the HER during EASH over CoPc/XCNT catalysts, the adsorption behavior of hydrogen intermediates (*H) at Co centers was identified as the critical factor of catalytic efficiency. Aligning with the Sabatier principle, excessively strong *H adsorption increases surface hydrogen coverage, blocking C2H2 access to active sites and impairing hydrogenation activity50. Conversely, overly weak *H adsorption fails to sustain C2H2 hydrogenation kinetics while favoring HER dominance. To quantify these interactions, crystal orbital Hamiltonian population (CCOHP) analysis was employed to probe the proposed bonding states of adsorbed *H on CoPc/XCNT (Fig. 4j). The *H adsorption strength correlated positively with the d-band center of Co in CoPc/XCNT. The CoPc/NCNT, with an intermediate d-band center, showed an optimal *H bonding energy, which could facilitate rapid hydrogen transfer during EASH while avoiding HER-driven deactivation caused by extreme *H coverage. Calculated H2O dissociation barriers and *H-binding Gibbs free energies further provided insights into potential mechanistic distinctions (Fig. 4k). Among the modeled CoPc/XCNT catalysts, CoPc/NCNT demonstrated a 3.20 eV lower H2O dissociation barrier alongside a 1.24 eV higher *H combination barrier. This dual energetic modulation is proposed to favor efficient *H generation via accelerated water activation while kinetically suppressing H2 formation. Consequently, abundant *H intermediates could participate selectively in C2H2 semi-hydrogenation, which aligns with the experimentally observed 86.7% FE and 99.99% selectivity for C2H4 at −500 mA cm⁻2, with complete suppression of C4 byproducts. Furthermore, a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the C2H2 hydrogenation process was then investigated by the Gibbs free-energy diagram for each elementary step (Fig. 4l and Supplementary Fig. S44). The first hydrogenation step (*C2H2 → *C2H3) of CoPc/OCNT, CoPc/NCNT, and CoPc/SCNT catalysts delivered limiting barriers of 0.61, 0.58, and 0.51 eV, respectively. This barrier hierarchy aligned with the onset potentials for C2H4 generation observed in online DEMS, supporting the idea that molecular regulation can act as an effective strategy to modulate EASH activity. Despite the more positive C2H4 generation potential of CoPc/OCNT, its EASH performance was limited by insufficient *H supply and unavoidable HER competition. In contrast, CoPc/NCNT achieved high activity through enhanced *H availability and utilization efficiency, while CoPc/SCNT suffered from severe HER interference. The calculated high energy barrier for *C2H4 → *C2H5 conversion (>0.2 eV) across CoPc/XCNT catalysts could explain the negligible C2H6 content experimentally observed in products (<0.6%), suggesting robust suppression of over-hydrogenation. These results collectively imply that the molecular strategy regulated EASH kinetics by tailoring the d-orbital electron occupancy of Co centers. CoPc/NCNT, with its intermediate d-band center, optimized *H adsorption and utilization, likely contributing to the highly efficient and selective acetylene reduction to ethylene over a wide current range.

Importantly, a similar coordination regulation also improves the performance of Cu phthalocyanine. Guided by the CoPc/NCNT design, we prepared an N-coordinated CuPc/NCNT analogue by immobilising CuPc on amino-functionalised CNTs using the same procedure as for CoPc/NCNT. In Ar saturated 1 M KOH, CuPc/NCNT displays a more positive HER onset potential and higher current density than CuPc/OCNT, which is consistent with more facile water dissociation at the Cu sites (Supplementary Fig. S45). Under EASH conditions, this enhanced water dissociation translates into higher ethylene selectivity and suppressed side reactions. At 100 mA cm⁻2, the Faradaic efficiency for C2H4 increases from 52.2 to 75.9% when moving from CuPc/OCNT to CuPc/NCNT, while the C2H6 FE decreases from 1.40 to 0.80% (Supplementary Fig. S46). Taken together with the CoPc/XCNT series, these observations indicate that axial coordination regulation provides a general route to improve water dissociation and to suppress competing HER and carbon–carbon coupling in MPc-based EASH catalysts, rather than being limited to the specific case of CoPc/NCNT.

Direct electroreduction of acetylene to high-purity ethylene

Motivated by its high FE for C2H4 and the selectivity, CoPc/NCNT catalysts were used for the direct conversion of C2H2 to high-purity C2H4 under practical operating conditions, including an ethylene-rich environment and a large work electrode area. Considering the low concentration of acetylene impurities in practical ethylene streams from cracked gas, the influence of acetylene concentration in the gas mixture on the EASH performance of CoPc/NCNT was first investigated in a 1.0 M KOH aqueous solution using a feed gas composed of argon and acetylene. The LSV curves of CoPc/NCNT exhibited a distinctly positive shift with increasing acetylene concentration (Supplementary Fig. S47). The FE for C2H4 at −100 mA cm-2 decreased from 96.6% under pure acetylene feed to 80.4% under 10% acetylene feed, resulting from the enhanced competition from HER caused by insufficient *H utilization for EASH (Fig. 5a). To satisfy the requirements for the industrial production of polymer-grade ethylene, the EASH performance was subsequently assessed under realistic conditions with ⁓0.5% acetylene impurities (5000 ppm) in crude ethylene. Lower inlet flow rates correspond to longer gas residence times on the catalyst surface. As shown in Fig. 5c, with a decrease in inlet flow rate, the increasing residence time of gas on CoPc/NCNT contributed to a higher conversion of C2H2. When the inlet flow rate was 20 sccm, the ethylene-specific selectivity was approximately 99%, nearly meeting the requirements of polymerized ethylene. Furthermore, during a 110 h stability test in a crude ethylene flow, both the acetylene conversion and specific selectivity of ethylene over CoPc/NCNT remained higher than 99.7% and 99.5%, respectively (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. S48). This good stability indicated the efficient EASH capability of CoPc/NCNT, even in a C2H4-rich environment with a low C2H2 partial pressure. The direct electroreduction of acetylene to a high concentration of ethylene was performed using a homemade tandem device consisting of a 1.0 cm2 flow cell and a 25 cm2 flow cell (Supplementary Fig. S49). The 1 cm2 flow cell was designed to deal with high-concentration C2H2 feed gas, and the 25 cm2 flow cell was used to convert residual C2H2 at low concentrations. Initially, pure C2H2 was pumped into the 1.0 cm2 flow cell, and the outlet gas was then immediately fed into the 25 cm2 flow cell without any purification (Fig. 5d). At the optimal flow rate of 4 mL min−1, the single-pass C2H2 conversion exceeded ~99%, and C2H4 selectivity surpassed 98%, respectively. A preliminary techno-economic analysis based on recently reported EASH models suggests that, under literature-consistent assumptions, this tandem configuration can operate within an economically reasonable regime (Supplementary Note 2). Taken together, these results underscore the practical potential of CoPc/NCNT for selective acetylene semi-hydrogenation and highlight the importance of molecular regulation in tuning the performance of molecular electrocatalysts.

In summary, a carbon nanotube-supported metal phthalocyanines, MPc/XCNT (M = Cu, Co, Ni, Fe; X = O, N, S), is developed as a useful platform to reveal the function of the metal identity and local coordination environment in the EASH. Comparative studies within the MPc/OCNT series demonstrate the key role of metal identity in enabling water activation to suppress C4 formation, with CoPc-based catalysts standing out for effectively promoting this step and achieving high ethylene selectivity. Building on this, a tunable molecular strategy is further adopted to modulate the coordination environment of CoPc-based catalysts. The optimized molecular regulation fine-tunes the d-band center of Co sites, modulating *H intermediate generation and utilization to mitigate HER and over-hydrogenation. The resulting CoPc/NCNT delivers competitive performance, achieving 86.7% ethylene FE with negligible ethane production (<0.01%) and no detectable C4H6 even at a large current density of 500 mA cm-2 under a pure C2H2 feed, and reaching 99.7% C2H2 conversion with up to 99.5% C2H4 selectivity under a simulated industrial crude C2H4 atmosphere. This work not only establishes the great capability of cobalt to reconcile C–C coupling suppression with selective hydrogenation but also provides a universal molecular strategy for tailoring the local coordination environment of molecular catalysts to advance electrocatalytic transformations.
paper_content.methods:
Chemicals and materials

Commerical CNT powder, cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc, 99.5%), phthalocyanine (Pc, 93.0%), N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.0%), anhydrous ethanol (CH3CH2OH, 99.9%), tert-butanol (99.5%), tetramethylammonium hydroxide (95%), deuterium oxide (99.0%), carbon nanotube (95.0%), (3-aminopropyl) triethoxysilane (95.0%), (3-mercaptopropyl)trimethoxysilane (95.0%), Nafion solution (5 wt%) were purchased from Aladdin Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 95.0%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 95%), potassium chloride (KCl, 99%), vitriol (H2SO4, 99%), were purchased from Sinopharm Co. Ltd. The GDL (SGL, 28BC), Pt foil (0.4-mm thickness), anion exchange membrane (fumasep FASB-PK-130) was purchased from Fuel Cell Store. The deionized water (>18.25 MΩ) was used for the experiments. All chemicals were used without further purification.

Preparation of functionalized carbon nanotubes

The hydroxyl-modified carbon nanotubes (OCNT) material was synthesized by chemically introducing oxygen functional groups onto the surface of the original carbon nanotubes (CNT) through an oxidation treatment using concentrated nitric acid (HNO3). In a typical procedure, 2.0 g of CNT powder was uniformly dispersed in 100 mL of 68 wt% HNO3 while being continuously stirred magnetically. The oxidation process was carried out at 140 °C for 12 hours, followed by thorough washing with water and subsequent freeze drying. It is crucial to manage the evaporation of concentrated HNO3 and any decomposition products using an ice water condenser. During this process, potential metal impurities present on the CNT surface were effectively removed through intensive acid etching. Amino-modified carbon nanotubes (NCNT) were synthesized as follows: 0.5 g of the prepared OCNT was dissolved in 100 mL of mixed solvent (Vethanol/Vwater = 9/1). After achieving good dispersion, 0.75 mL of (3-aminopropyl) triethoxysilane was added dropwise under vigorous stirring. After that, the black solution was kept at 60 °C for 10 h. The product was washed with deionized water several times and freeze-dried for 24 h. Sulfhydryl-modified carbon nanotubes (SCNT) were synthesized using the same method by replacing (3-Aminopropyl)triethoxysilane with (3-mercaptopropyl)trimethoxysilane.

Preparation of catalysts

CoPc/NCNT and Pc/NCNT catalysts were synthesized using a simple impregnation method at 25 °C. Typically, NCNT (100 mg) and CoPc (5 mg) were dispersed in a strong polar solvent of DMF solution (100 mL) and stirred for 20 h, followed by separation and freeze-drying treatments. By adjusting the mass percent ratio of CoPc and NCNT using 1, 5, or 10 mg CoPc with fixed 100 mg NCNT, CoPc/NCNT-1, CoPc/NCNT-5, and CoPc/NCNT-10 were prepared. Similarly, FePc/OCNT, NiPc/OCNT, CuPc/OCNT, CuPc/NCNT, CoPc/OCNT, and CoPc/SCNT were also synthesized in parallel by the same method as the CoPc/NCNT catalyst, except for replacing NCNT with OCNT and SCNT, respectively. Meanwhile, CoPc/CNT was prepared using the original CNT as support.

Fabrication of electrodes

The electrodes used in this work were prepared using a traditional drop-coating technique. 6.0 mg of the catalyst powder was dispersed in 5 mL of an ethanol-water mixture (Vethanol/Vwater = 4/1) with sonication for 1 h. Then, 20 μl of Nafion solution (5 wt%) was added to the solution for another 0.5 h. Subsequently, the commercial GDE (SGL, 28BC) was cut into a rectangular shape with a size of 1 × 3 cm2 to serve as the electrode substrate. The influence of mass loading per geometric area on acetylene-to-ethylene performance was assessed by varying the catalyst loading on the GDL to 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 mg cm−2 (Supplementary Figs. S22). Unless otherwise specified, the catalyst loading of 0.4 mg cm−2 on the GDL was used for the MPc/XCNT catalysts in subsequent experiments; the mass loading of bare CoPc on the GDL was matched to that of CoPcs in the CoPc/XCNT catalysts on the GDL, specifically 0.06 mg cm−2. The as-prepared electrodes were dried at 25 °C.

Electrochemical measurements in the flow cell

Electrochemical measurements were performed in a divided three-compartment electrochemical cell with a window area of 1 cm2 (2 × 0.5 cm2), which consists of a gas chamber, cathodic chamber, and anodic chamber. Generally, GDE with a catalyst as the working electrode, Pt foil as the counter-electrode, and Hg/HgO as the reference electrode constituted an electrocatalytic system using the Gamry 5000 electrochemical workstation. The cathodic and anodic compartments, both containing 1.0 M KOH electrolyte, were separated by an anion exchange membrane (FAB-PK-130). The 1.0 M KOH electrolyte was freshly prepared using ultrapure water and stored in a sealed polyethylene bottle. The cell resistance was determined prior to the electrochemical measurements using the built-in high-frequency impedance technique of the electrochemical workstation. The electrochemical surface area (ECSA) was estimated using the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) method. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted in a non-faradaic region from −0.05 to 0.05 V vs. RHE at varying scan rates (20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, and 140 mV s−1). The Cdl values were determined by plotting the charging current density difference (Δj = ja –jc) at 0 V vs. RHE against the scan rates, where the slope of the linear fit represents twice the value of Cdl.

All LSV curves were iR compensated with a compensation level of 70%. All potentials were converted to the RHE scale according to Eq. (1).

E = EHg/HgO + 0.098 + 0.059 × pH (1)

For the three-electrode flow cell system operated under pure C2H2, a reactor with an electrode area of 1 cm2 was used. The cathode gas chamber was supplied with pure C2H2 at a flow rate of 20 ml min−1, while 1 M KOH (PH=14.0) was pumped around both the cathode and anode sides at a flow rate of 20 ml min−1. The potentials presented in this system were cell voltages (Ecell).

Three-electrode flow cell systems (5 × 5 cm2), which consist of CoPc/NCNT GDE, Pt foil, and Hg/HgO electrodes, were used with 15 mL of 1 M KOH. Chronoamperometry was performed at −40 mA cm−2 and 10 mL min−1 to purify ethylene from ethylene-rich simulated gas (0.5% C2H2, 20% C2H4 balanced with Ar). Electrolyte flow rate set at 5 mL min−1. Prior to quantitative analysis, the electrochemical semihydrogenation of acetylene was stabilized for 5–10 minutes under varying current densities. Following this stabilization, the effluent from the flow cell was directly introduced into a gas chromatograph for product analysis.

In the tandem flow cell configuration, comprising a fore-cell (1 cm2) and a post-cell (25 cm2), 100% C2H2 gas entered the fore-cell and was partially converted to a C2H4 and C2H2 mixture at −500 mA cm⁻2 with a flow rate of 4 mL min⁻1. The fore-cell’s outlet gas was immediately fed into the post-cell via a short connection to minimize dead volume. In the post-cell, residual C2H2 was converted to C2H4 at −40 mA cm−2 and 4 mL min⁻1. Individual pumps provided 1 M KOH electrolyte to the tandem system at 10 mL min−1. All the electrochemical performances are presented without the iR compensation except for LSV tests.

Electrochemical operando online DEMS analysis

In-situ differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) analysis was performed using a Linglu Instruments QAS 100LiA system (Iridium filament, 5*10‒4 A/mbar). A detailed schematic of the DEMS electrochemical cell is provided in Fig. 4e. Given that all products of the EASH process are gaseous, this setup enabled real-time monitoring of product distribution, thereby directly elucidating selectivity. The single-cell reactor was coupled to the DEMS via a quartz capillary inserted into its outlet, which interfaced with a PTFE membrane (Gore-Tex, 0.22 μm) to selectively transfer the gaseous effluent into the negatively pressurized DEMS gas circuit. Electrochemical performance was evaluated using a CHI760E workstation, with linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) conducted from 0 to −0.5 V vs. RHE. The mass-to-charge ratios (m/z) of 2, 26, 28, 30, and 54 were assigned to H2, C2H2, C2H4, C2H6, and C4H6, respectively. Raw ion currents are plotted on absolute intensity scales without mathematical correction or deconvolution, as data collection began only after baseline stabilization.

Electrochemical in situ FTIR spectra measurements

In situ FTIR measurements were conducted using a Nicolet IS50 spectrometer equipped with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled MCT-A detector. A gold-coated Ge prism served as the working electrode, prepared via sputter-coating (Quorum SC7620) at 30 mA for 60 s to ensure a uniform conductive surface. Before each experiment, a CoPc/NCNT ink was deposited onto a gold film that was pre-coated on the Ge prism. A standard three-electrode configuration was employed, utilizing a Pt wire counter electrode and a Hg/HgO reference electrode. The measurements were performed in a 1.0 M KOH electrolyte, which was pre-saturated and continuously purged with C2H2. Potentiostatic IR spectra were acquired using a CHI760E workstation over a potential range from the open-circuit potential to −1.2 V. Spectra were synchronously collected from 4000 to 650 cm−1 with a 4 cm−1 resolution.

Electrochemical in situ XANES spectra measurements

In situ XANES measurements at the Co K-edge were performed using an ultra-high flux benchtop X-ray absorption fine structure spectrometer (RapidXAFS 2M, Anhui Absorption Spectroscopy Analysis Instrument Co., Ltd.). The instrument was operated at 20 kV and 40 mA and equipped with a Si (533) spherically bent crystal analyzer (radius of curvature: 500 mm), which serves for energy selection of the incident X-ray beam and enables rapid acquisition of XANES spectra under operando conditions. The measurements were conducted using a specially designed H-type electrolytic cell, with electrode configurations and reaction conditions identical to those in the performance tests. The spectra were acquired under a continuous gas flow. Initially, data were collected at the open-circuit potential (OCP) after purging the electrolyte with Ar or acetylene for 40 minutes. Subsequently, spectra were recorded after applying a series of potentials, each for a duration of 10 minutes.

Electrochemical quasi-in situ EPR measurements

Quasi-in situ electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra were recorded at 25 °C on an X-band Bruker EMX microspectrometer. The instrument was configured with the following parameters: center field = 3500 G, sweep width = 100 G, sweep time = 5 min, modulation amplitude = 1 G, and microwave attenuation = 20 mW. For electrochemical EPR measurements, the 1 cm2 flow cell integrated a three-electrode system, separated by a proton exchange membrane (FAB-PK-130), with Hg/HgO and Pt foil serving as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. Potentials were applied using a Gamry 5000 electrochemical workstation. Sample solutions containing DMPO were loaded into quartz tubes for analysis, while the electrolyte was purged with ultrapure Ar for at least 30 minutes before measurements to ensure an anoxic environment.

Performance assessment

Gas products (C2H4, C2H2, C4, H2) were analyzed through gas chromatography (Fuli, 9790PLUS) coupled with a FID detector and a TCD detector. The Plot Al2O3 column separated ethylene, acetylene, and C4, while the Molecular Sieve 5 A columns separated H2. An external standard method was applied to estimate the concentration of the component of gas products (Supplementary Fig. S50). The calculation of the C2H2 conversion and the evolution rate of different products was performed using equations (2) and (3), and the FEs of different products were calculated using equation (4). Turnover frequency (TOF) for C2H4 (−500 mA cm−2) was calculated using equation (5):

Conversion (%) = (cfeed - c') / cfeed × 100% (2)

Selectivity (%) = (cfeed - c') / (cfeed ‒ c' + cC2H6 +2 × cC4) × 100% (3)

FE (%) = (n × m × F) / (I × t) × 100% (4)

TOF (min−1) = (amount of C2H4 molecules produced per min) / (amount of Co sites) (5)

Where, cfeed: concentration of C2H2 feed gas, c', cC2H6, cC4: the concentration of C2H2, C2H6, C4 in gas products. n: number of transferred electrons, m: amount of substance, F: Faraday’s constant, I: total current, t: electrolysis time. All data points with error bars represent the mean ± standard deviation from three independent measurements.

Characterization

The phase structure was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’Pert PRO MPD) using Cu Kα radiation (λ= 1.518 Å). The morphology of the catalysts was measured by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Thermo Scientific Talos F200X). High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were carried out on a spherical aberration-corrected microscope (Titan 80-300). The chemical constituents of the catalysts were studied by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) with an Mg Kα radiation (1486.6 eV) monochromatic X-ray source (Thermo Scientific Escalab 250XI). The cobalt content was detected by an Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometer (ICP-OES) (Agilent 5110). The hydrogen temperature-programmed desorption (H2-TPD) was conducted on a TP-5080 apparatus equipped with a thermal conductivity detector. X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) was carried out at 1W1B station in Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility (BSRF). The acquired EXAFS data were processed and analyzed using the ATHENA module of the IFEFFIT software package following standard procedures. Co foil, CoO, and Co3O4 were used as reference standards to determine the valence state and coordination environment of Co in the catalysts.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations

All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were executed utilizing the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)51. The electron exchange and correlation effects were treated through the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional. A plane-wave kinetic energy cutoff was set to 450 eV. For the CoPc surface models, the Brillouin zone was sampled using a 3×3×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh, selected based on the supercell dimensions. A vacuum region of more than 15 Å was incorporated along the z-direction to prevent spurious interactions between periodic slabs. Structural relaxations were carried out until the electronic energy and the Hellmann-Feynman forces on each atom converged to within 10⁻5 eV and 0.01 eV/Å, respectively. These specific parameters were finalized following rigorous total energy convergence tests52. Transition state (TS) searches were performed using the Dimer method in the VTST package53. This involved generating initial guess geometries with the climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method, followed by convergence to the saddle points using the Dimer method. All optimized structures were verified to have atomic forces less than 0.1 eV Å−1. The optimized atomic coordinates structures are provided as Supplementary Data 154.

The adsorption energy (Eads) of reaction intermediates and the free energy change can be computed using equations (6)-(7):

ΔEads = Esys – Esurface – Eadsorb (6)

ΔG = ΔE + ΔEDFT + ΔEZPE – TΔS (7)

where Esys is the energy of the system with surface and adsorbate, Esurface is the energy of the catalyst surface, and Eadsorb corresponds to the energy of the isolated adsorbate. ΔG, ΔE, ΔEDFT, ΔEZPE, and TΔS stand for, respectively, the free energy, total energy from DFT calculations, zero-point energy, and entropic contributions.

The C2H2 hydrogenation process to C2H4 can be delineated by equations (9)-(11):

* + C2H2 → *C2H2 (9)

*C2H2 + H+ + e− → *C2H3 (10)

*C2H3 + H+ + e− → *C2H4 (11)

The hydrogen combination proceeded through equations (12)-(13):

* + 2H → 2*H (12)

*H + *H → *H2 (13)

The C-C coupling proceeded through this equation (14):

2*C2H3 → *C4H6 (14)

While the water dissociation proceeded through equations (15)-(18):

* + H2O → *H2O (15)

*H2O → *H‒OH (16)

*H‒OH → *H + *OH (17)

*H + *OH → *H + OH (18)

Data availability

The Source Data file and Supplementary Data 1 have been deposited in Figshare under accession code DOI link54. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31622623.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript titled “Molecular Cobalt Catalysts for Highly Selective Electrocatalytic Acetylene Semi-Hydrogenation” investigates the electrocatalytic semi-hydrogenation of acetylene using cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) supported on differently functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs). The authors compare CoPc with CuPc catalysts, and systematically study the effect of O-, S-, and N-doped CNT supports on catalytic activity. To elucidate the reaction mechanism of CoPc/NCNT, they employ a broad range of techniques, including in situ XANES, FTIR, EPR, DEMS, and DFT calculations. Additional characterization methods such as TEM, Raman spectroscopy, and kinetic isotope effect studies are also used. Finally, they demonstrate the direct electroreduction of acetylene to high concentrations of ethylene in a homemade tandem device, combining a 1 cm2 flow cell with a 25 cm2 flow cell. Overall, the study is interesting and represents a meaningful contribution to the field of electrocatalytic acetylene semi-hydrogenation. However, the manuscript currently suffers from missing experimental details, insufficient depth in some aspects of the data analysis, and a lack of clarity in the presentation of certain results and writing. Before the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications, the following comments must be thoroughly addressed:
1. On page 4, at the beginning of the Results and Discussion section, additional experimental details are required. For example, the electrolyte conditions should be specified when introducing the LSV data (“Under an Ar atmosphere, the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of the CoPc/OCNT demonstrated both a more positive onset potential and higher current density across the HER polarization range compared with those of CuPc/OCNT”). The writing should also be more quantitative: rather than stating “a more positive onset potential,” the authors should report the exact numerical difference. Similarly, when presenting selectivity values, the amounts of by-products (e.g. C4 species) should be given. On page 6, the phrase “consistent with the earlier onset potentials observed in LSV measurements” should be clarified by specifying the actual onset potential shift.
2. Throughout the manuscript, the authors tend to draw conclusions too rapidly, and the hypotheses should be formulated more carefully. For example, on page 5 the statement that CoPc/OCNT exhibits “facilitated water dissociation and thus enhanced EASH performance” is not sufficiently supported, as LSV data alone only demonstrate higher or earlier activity and do not provide direct evidence of water dissociation. Similarly, on page 10 the claim that “the variations in polarization curves and selectivity clearly indicated that the ESAH kinetics and reaction pathway on CoPc/XCNT could be effectively tuned by modulating the X heteroatom electronegativity” is overstated, since the correlation with electronegativity remains speculative without additional mechanistic evidence.
3. On page 6, the discussion of water dissociation barriers and Gibbs free energy for *H binding is confusing. The authors state that CoPc/OCNT exhibits stronger H2O dissociation and a higher barrier for *H coupling, resulting in slower HER kinetics (Figure 1h). However, this appears inconsistent with the earlier LSV and DEMS results, where CoPc/OCNT was described as facilitating the reaction. The authors should reconcile these two observations and clarify how they are connected.
4. Regarding the characterization, for Figure S8, reference pattern should be provided for the XRD data. In addition, there is an inconsistency in Figure S9: the main text refers to FTIR, while the SI shows a Raman spectrum. Also, according to the literature, CoPc can typically be detected in the lower wavenumber region (600–700 cm-1) with Raman, which does not overlap with CNT vibrations (see J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 14, 12298–12307, Fig. S13). The authors should carefully examine this region. For Xanes, reference spectra of bare CoPc in Figure S13 should be provided for comparison.
5. For the AC-STEM images (Figures 2d and S12), the legend for the 3D heat map is missing and should be provided with length-scale if possible.
6. In general, it would be important to include error bars, for example in the ICP-OES data, to highlight the reproducibility of the synthesis and Co loading. Likewise, Table S2 for the EXAFS Fits should report explicit error values rather than only providing a general description below the table.
7. For the explanation of the XANES-data in Figure 2f the authors should provide a clearer explanation of the significance of the pre-edge shift observed and how this correlates with the different CNTs.
8. The SI should also include the measured electrode potentials. In Figure 3e, it is unclear whether Ecell refers to the working electrode potential or the total cell voltage, this should be specified. In the Methods section, all potentials are described as iR-corrected, yet in the SI no such correction appears to be applied. Please provide the typical ohmic drop values. Additionally, in many current density plots in the SI (e.g. Figure S17), the authors note “The results are presented without iR compensation”, but since no potential values are shown in the graphs, this statement is not meaningful.
9. On page 10, the statement “Impressively, at an industrial-level current density of 500 mA cm-2, the FE for C2H4 remained above 85%, continuing to fall within the profitable region and indicating the excellent economic potential of the CoPc/NCNT catalyst towards EASH (Figure S18)” requires clarification. How is the “profitable region” defined, and what is the energy efficiency of the reaction under these conditions? What metrics are truly required for industrial application? Moreover, Figure S18 shows GC data, which does not support this economic claim. On page 11, the stability discussion is also incomplete. The authors show that at 100 mA cm-2 the catalyst remains stable for 60 h (Figure 3e), but no data are provided at 500 mA cm-2, which would be necessary to support claims of industrial relevance.
10. The authors compare CoPc with supported CoPc on OCNT, SCNT, and NCNT. However, a direct comparison with CoPc on bare CNTs is missing. Including this control is important to clearly demonstrate the necessity and benefit of CNT functionalization.
11. In Figure S22, the data for the lowest loading and lowest current appear significantly different and may represent an outlier. Is this result reproducible? On page 11, the authors state that CoPc/NCNT with 5 wt% CoPc and a loading of 0.4 mg cm-2 was used and gave the best electrocatalytic performance. How does this loading on CNT and catalyst loading compare with other reports on CoPc–CNT systems, for example in CO2RR to CO or methanol? Is the chosen loading consistent with the literature, or does it need to be specifically adjusted for the present reaction? What kind of GDE is used?
12. Regarding the change in Co oxidation state observed by in situ XANES: can the authors provide clearer insights into the specific oxidation state transition (e.g., from which to which state)? The statement “This valence reduction was correlated with electron transfer from Co to adsorbed C2H2 species, facilitating rapid acetylene reduction and clearly confirming Co as the primary active site” is difficult to follow. Is this conclusion directly supported by the presented data, or is it primarily drawn from the literature?
13. The peak assignments of the in situ FTIR data in Figure 4b do not align with the cited reference. The authors assign the bands at 1650 and 1559 cm-1 to the *C≡C bond of C2H2 and the generated *C=C bond adsorbed on CoPc/NCNT, respectively. However, according to the reference, adsorbed *C2H2 species can be detected at 1641 cm-1 over ED–Cu NPs, while the band at 1577 cm-1 corresponds to *C2H3, the key intermediate of C2H2 hydrogenation. Therefore, a more consistent assignment according to that reference would be 1650 cm-1 to *C2H2 and 1559 cm-1 to *C2H3. This interpretation would also better match the observed peak evolution, where the 1650 cm-1 band increases at higher overpotentials. Are these overpotential-dependent changes correlated with product selectivity? Furthermore, do the relative intensity changes of these two peaks align with the expected reaction pathway? The authors should also examine whether additional informative spectral regions around 2000 cm-1 are present in the FTIR spectra.
14. On page 13, the discussion of pH variation and radical scavenger experiments is too brief and the conclusions are drawn too quickly. The pH was only varied slightly (from ~13.7 to ~14.3), which corresponds to a relatively small change in OH- concentration. The authors should also specify which concentrations of KOH corresponds to which pH. In addition, when introducing t-BuOH as a radical scavenger, the exact concentration used (50 mM) should be reported in the main text. This is a relatively high concentration, and it should be clarified whether the observed effect can be attributed specifically to radical scavenging or to other interactions with the system.
15. The reported EASH reaction kinetics follow the trend K+ > Na+ > TMA+, with C2H2 conversion decreasing from K+ to 10.4% TMA+. How does this trend compare with previous literature? Have larger or smaller cations such as Cs+ or Li+ been tested? It is worth noting that molecular catalysts often exhibit very different cation-dependent effects compared to metallic catalysts (see Yu, S., Yamauchi, H., Wang, S. et al. Nat. Catal. 7, 1000–1009 (2024)).
16. More details about the gas feed are required. Was the acetylene introduced in ethylene or in argon? More details about the gas feed mixing is required. Additional clarification is also needed on the 1 cm2 and 25 cm2 flow cell setups, how exactly are they configured and operated? In the text, the authors state: “To satisfy the requirements for the industrial production of polymer-grade ethylene, the EASH performance was subsequently assessed under realistic conditions with 0.5% acetylene impurities (5000 ppm) in crude ethylene (Figure S33).” However, Figure S33 shows LSV curves of different gas concentrations.
17. The Methods section requires substantial revision, as both the main text and the Supporting Information currently provide too few details to ensure reproducibility. The experimental procedures should be described comprehensively, including complete information on catalyst synthesis and functionalization (precursors, solvents, conditions, purification), electrode preparation and loading (mass loading, electrode area, binder composition, deposition procedure), and electrochemical testing protocols (cell configuration, electrolyte composition and preparation, gas feed composition and flow rates, reference and counter electrode details, iR compensation). In addition, the in situ and operando experiments (XANES, FTIR, EPR, DEMS) must be described in sufficient detail, including setups, acquisition parameters, and data analysis methods. Calibration and quantification procedures (e.g., GC, ICP-OES) should also be reported, together with error analysis and reproducibility tests. Without this level of detail, the results cannot be reliably reproduced, and the section must therefore be carefully revised and expanded to meet the standards of Nature Communications.
Minor comments:
-Page 5, ESAE should be ESAH.
-The authors should write the minus sign for the current densities (I assume negative currents were applied).
-Hard to distinguish the colors (such as blue and green) in many of the plots.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work, the authors report a molecular cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc) catalyst platform that promotes electrocatalytic acetylene semi-hydrogenation (EASH) reaction activity through electronic regulation. They also investigate the performance modulation strategies and reaction mechanisms of the corresponding molecular catalysts. The utilization of analogous molecular catalysts (CoPc and CuPc) for EASH catalysis have been previously reported [10.1016/j.cej.2021.134129]. Moreover, the authors' research and conclusions on the performance enhancement mechanism of CoPc/XCNT are not sufficiently clear. Therefore, I do not recommend publishing this work in Nature Communications.
1.Apart from the already reported feasibility of metal phthalocyanines in the EASH process, the employed CoPc/OCNT and CuPc/OCNT are also widely used in various electrocatalytic reactions including CO2RR, ORR, HER, and etc. (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202310623; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2021, 50, 12985; Nature, 2019, 575, 639). By simply combining the two points together, the present work is lack of innovation to be published in Nature Communications.
2.Except for the novelty issue, the data and analysis is not adequately to support their hypothesis and conclusions. For example, to exclude the CPET pathway, the author claimed that “the pH was varied from ~13.7 to ~14.3, negligible changes were observed in the polarization curves and FE for C2H4 on CoPc/NCNT”, which is contradictory to the data shown in Figure S27.
3.In Page 13, the authors claimed that a hydrogen transfer mechanism could bypass the HER competitive, which is groundless. It has been widely reported that H2 could also obtained by the combination of two water-derived *H, called Tafel step (J. Phys. Chem. C, 2018, 122, 23943.). Thus, the real reason for the improved C2H4 selectivity is not the claimed mechanism, which needs further discussion.
4.The observed performance disparities between CoPC/NCTN and other samples are predominantly attributable to the difference in water dissociation ability. However, this seems inconsistent with the kinetic isotope experiment results for catalysts. The LSV or kinetic isotope experiment results for catalysts under argon gas should be provided for further comparison.
5.The as-reported TOF value is too high to convince the reviewer. According to the data in the previous literature (Chem. Eng. J. 2022, 431, 134129), the bare CoPc only exhibited a TOF value of 0.29 min-1 at a current of 100 mA. How can the TOF of the as-reported CoPc/NCNT reach 9700 min-1 at a current of 500 mA? More details are needed for the TOF calculation. Besides, the claimed 24 h continuous operation under ethylene-rich simulated gas flow could not be regarded as an advancement compared to the recent progress (Nat. Catal.2021, 4, 557; 10.31635/ccschem.024.202404849; 10.1002/anie.202509501; 10.31635/ccschem.022.202101750;)
6.In Figure 1g, comparing the d-band centers of different metals is quite uncommon and meaningless. Meanwhile, in Figures 1h, I and 4k, the author employed unusual plotting methods to present the reaction diagrams, which resulted in poorer data readability and a higher likelihood of misinterpretation. For example, in the conventional *H generation process, it is necessary to calculate the steady-state *H2O and *H+*OH as the initial and final states of the water dissociation process, as well as the corresponding transition states, while considering the *OH desorption process. It is very incomplete for the author to only calculate the energy barrier from *H2O to *H+*OH. The generation processes of H2 and C4 also face similar issues.
7.The manuscript does not present any calculation methods, and lacks the display of relevant and representative adsorption models. For single-atom catalysts, the selection of adsorption sites is crucial and needs to be demonstrated. In the processes of water dissociation and hydrogenation, it is necessary to clarify whether C and O species occupy the metal sites, and where *H is adsorbed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this work, the authors report a CoPc-OCNT catalyst towards EASH, achieving FE of 86.7% under 500 mA cm-2. The manuscript attributes the enhanced activity to the excellent hydrogenation ability of CoPc, but similar arguments were already reported in prior studies (Chem. Eng. J. 2022, 431: 134129). Therefore, the reviewer considers the current form of this work lacks of novelty and not suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
1. The authors choose the CoPc/OCNT as the model catalyst due to its better ability of water dissociation. How about NiPc/OCNT and FePc/OCNT, which has been proved the great activity on water dissociation. Besides, the FE of C2H4 decreased and FE of H2 increased sharply under high current densities, suggesting the inferior ability of CoPC/OCNT to tune the *H. The authors propose the CoPc/OCNT can inhibit C-C coupling to generate C4 byproducts, while the key Co sites may have no activity on C-C coupling.
2. The authors use the different carbon substrate (N-CNT, S-CNT, O-CNT) to tune coordination of Co center and optimize its catalytic performance. How about the performance of CoPc/CNT without doping? The CoPc/NCNT achieves the better performance. The authors should prove the increased performance is not originate the change of physical properties (conductivity, hydrophilicity, adsorption capacity).
3. The most electrochemical results presented in this study lack error bars, which may raise concerns about the reproducibility and reliability of the reported data.
4. The in-situ FT-IR data presented in this study are underexplored. The analysis of water peaks range from 3000-4000 cm-1 may be benefit of revealing the tune of water dissociation.
5. The selectivity performance using t-BuOH in electrolyte should be provide to the demonstrate the role of *H, while the LSV curves are not enough.
6. The authors design a tandem system to generate high-purity C2H4. However, the reviewer wants know if such a design has practical significance.
